snapshots.name: Sherlock Holmes
snapshots.subtitle: The consulting detective
snapshots.body: A private consulting detective with rooms in Baker Street, London. Clients bring him problems the police cannot solve or will not touch; his friend Dr. Watson narrates the cases.

snapshots.name: Dr. Watson
snapshots.subtitle: Holmes’s friend and the narrator
snapshots.body: A doctor and Holmes’s former fellow lodger at Baker Street, who tells these stories. He is now married and has returned to medical practice, but still joins Holmes on his cases.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mrs. Hudson
snapshots.subtitle: Of the Baker Street household
snapshots.body: A member of the household at Holmes’s Baker Street rooms, mentioned by Holmes in passing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Irene Adler
snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: A retired American-born opera singer living in London. Watson says she is the one woman Holmes always calls ‘the woman’, though not out of love.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Irene Adler
snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, born in New Jersey in 1858, once prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw and now retired and living in London. The King of Bohemia, who calls her an adventuress, had an affair with her when he was Crown Prince and wants back the letters and photograph she has.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Irene Adler
snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, formerly prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw, now living at Briony Lodge, St. John’s Wood. She holds a compromising photograph of herself with the King of Bohemia. She has just married the lawyer Godfrey Norton in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica, with Holmes, in his groom’s disguise, pulled in as witness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Irene Adler
snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born opera singer who outwits Holmes. She saw through his clergyman act after the fire alarm, followed him home in men’s clothes to wish him good night, and left England with her new husband, Godfrey Norton. In her letter, signed ‘Irene Norton, née Adler’, she promises not to trouble the King, keeping the photograph only for her own protection.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: King of Bohemia
snapshots.subtitle: Hereditary King of Bohemia
snapshots.body: The thirty-year-old hereditary King of Bohemia, of the House of Ormstein, who has come from Prague incognito to consult Holmes in person.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: King of Bohemia
snapshots.subtitle: Hereditary King of Bohemia
snapshots.body: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, the thirty-year-old hereditary King of Bohemia, in London incognito. He is about to announce his betrothal to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen and wants Holmes to recover a compromising photograph of himself with Irene Adler, which she has threatened to send to his bride’s family.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: King of Bohemia
snapshots.subtitle: Hereditary King of Bohemia
snapshots.body: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, hereditary King of Bohemia. Irene Adler’s letter convinces him she will never use the photograph, and he declares himself satisfied. He gives Holmes her portrait as a reward; Holmes takes it but coldly ignores the King’s outstretched hand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Count Von Kramm
snapshots.subtitle: Name given by a masked Bohemian visitor
snapshots.body: The name given to Holmes by a masked, very tall visitor with a strong German accent, who says he is a Bohemian nobleman.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Count Von Kramm (the King of Bohemia)
snapshots.subtitle: Name given by a masked Bohemian visitor
snapshots.body: A false name. The masked visitor who called himself Count Von Kramm, a Bohemian nobleman, is the King of Bohemia himself. He tears off his mask after Holmes addresses him as ‘your Majesty’, and he goes on using the name while staying at the Langham.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Slim youth in an ulster
snapshots.subtitle: Passer-by who greets Holmes in Baker Street
snapshots.body: A slim young man in an ulster who hurries past Holmes’s door in Baker Street at night and wishes him good night by name. Holmes is sure he has heard the voice before.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Slim youth in an ulster (Irene Adler)
snapshots.subtitle: Passer-by who greets Holmes in Baker Street
snapshots.body: Irene Adler in men’s clothes. After the fire alarm she suspected the clergyman, put on what she calls her ‘walking clothes’, followed Holmes home to make sure who he was, and then wished him good night.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Godfrey Norton
snapshots.subtitle: Lawyer of the Inner Temple
snapshots.body: A dark, handsome lawyer of the Inner Temple and Irene Adler’s only regular male visitor, who calls at Briony Lodge once or twice a day.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Godfrey Norton
snapshots.subtitle: Lawyer of the Inner Temple
snapshots.body: A dark, handsome lawyer of the Inner Temple who has just married Irene Adler in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica, with the disguised Holmes dragged in as their witness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Godfrey Norton
snapshots.subtitle: Lawyer of the Inner Temple
snapshots.body: A lawyer of the Inner Temple and Irene Adler’s new husband. The morning after the wedding the couple leave England for the Continent on the 5:15 train from Charing Cross.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen
snapshots.subtitle: Second daughter of the King of Scandinavia
snapshots.body: The second daughter of the King of Scandinavia, from a family of strict principles, whom the King of Bohemia is about to marry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John
snapshots.subtitle: Irene Adler’s coachman
snapshots.body: The coachman who drives Irene Adler’s landau.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mrs. Turner
snapshots.subtitle: Landlady at Baker Street in this story
snapshots.body: The landlady at the Baker Street lodgings, who brings Holmes a tray of supper.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Elderly servant at Briony Lodge
snapshots.subtitle: Servant at Briony Lodge
snapshots.body: An elderly woman on the steps of Briony Lodge who watches Holmes’s party with a sardonic eye and greets him by name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Clergyman at St. Monica’s
snapshots.subtitle: Clergyman at the Church of St. Monica
snapshots.body: The clergyman in a surplice at the Church of St. Monica in the Edgeware Road, seen arguing with a couple at the altar.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary Jane
snapshots.subtitle: Watson’s servant girl
snapshots.body: The clumsy, careless servant girl in Watson’s household, whom his wife has given notice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Hare
snapshots.subtitle: English stage actor
snapshots.body: An English actor of Watson’s day, named as the only performer who could have equalled Holmes in a part.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jabez Wilson
snapshots.subtitle: Red-headed pawnbroker and Holmes’s client
snapshots.body: A stout, elderly pawnbroker with blazing red hair who runs a small business in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City. He has come to Holmes with a strange story about a newspaper advertisement.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jabez Wilson
snapshots.subtitle: Red-headed pawnbroker and Holmes’s client
snapshots.body: A stout, elderly red-headed pawnbroker from Saxe-Coburg Square. Hired by the Red-Headed League to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica for £4 a week, he worked eight weeks until he found the office locked and a card announcing that the League was dissolved.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding
snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant at the pawnshop. Wilson says he is very capable and could earn twice as much elsewhere, but works for half wages to learn the business.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding
snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant, who works for half wages to learn the business. He showed Wilson the Red-Headed League’s advertisement, urged him to apply, and pushed him through the crowd of applicants. Wilson’s only complaint is his passion for photography, which keeps him in the cellar developing pictures.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding
snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant: a small, quick, beardless man of about thirty with an acid stain on his forehead and pierced ears. He showed Wilson the League’s advertisement and pushed him to apply. After a brief look at him, Holmes calls him the fourth smartest man in London and says he has known something of him before.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding (John Clay)
snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: The name John Clay used while working as Jabez Wilson’s assistant. Holmes explains that he took the job at half wages, urged Wilson to apply to the sham League, and used the hours Wilson was away to dig a tunnel from the cellar to the bank behind the shop.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A young master criminal—murderer, thief, coiner and forger—whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard names as the man he most wants to arrest. Jones says Clay has royal ancestry, went to Eton and Oxford, and has never been seen by him despite years of pursuit.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard has hunted for years. Holmes names him as the clean-cut, boyish young man who climbs up through the floor of the bank cellar.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard has hunted for years. Caught climbing up through the floor of the bank cellar, he is handcuffed by Jones, insists on his royal blood, and is led off coolly to the police station.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal caught tunnelling into the bank cellar and arrested by Peter Jones. Holmes explains that Clay, under the name Vincent Spaulding, had worked as Jabez Wilson’s assistant and devised the Red-Headed League with a red-haired accomplice to get Wilson out of the shop each day.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ross
snapshots.subtitle: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office
snapshots.body: The man named in the Red-Headed League’s newspaper advertisement as the person to apply to at the League’s offices, 7 Pope’s Court, Fleet Street.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ross
snapshots.subtitle: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office
snapshots.body: A small man with hair even redder than Jabez Wilson’s, who interviews the applicants at 7 Pope’s Court, chooses Wilson, and says he is himself a pensioner of the League’s fund.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ross
snapshots.subtitle: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office
snapshots.body: The red-headed man who hired Jabez Wilson for the Red-Headed League. After the League closed, the landlord said he had never heard the name: he knew the tenant as William Morris, a solicitor, and the forwarding address turned out to be a factory where nobody knew either name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ross
snapshots.subtitle: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office
snapshots.body: The man who ran the Red-Headed League’s office and hired Jabez Wilson. Holmes explains that the League was a scheme by John Clay and his red-haired accomplice to keep Wilson away from his shop: one rogue kept the temporary office while the other urged Wilson to apply.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: William Morris
snapshots.subtitle: Name the Pope’s Court landlord gives for the League office’s tenant
snapshots.body: The name the landlord at 7 Pope’s Court gives for the red-headed man who rented the room used as the League’s office—the man Jabez Wilson knew as Duncan Ross. The landlord says he was a solicitor who moved out the day before.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Morris
snapshots.subtitle: Name the Pope’s Court landlord gives for the League office’s tenant
snapshots.body: The name the landlord at 7 Pope’s Court gives for the red-headed tenant Jabez Wilson knew as Duncan Ross. The forwarding address, 17 King Edward Street, proved to be an artificial-kneecap factory where no one had heard of either name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Archie
snapshots.subtitle: Red-haired man in the bank cellar
snapshots.body: A small, pale young man with a shock of very red hair who is pulled up through the cellar floor by the first intruder. His companion calls him Archie.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archie
snapshots.subtitle: Red-haired man in the bank cellar
snapshots.body: The small, pale, red-haired man who came up through the cellar floor with John Clay and dived back down the hole when Holmes sprang. Holmes says three men were waiting at the house’s door, and that Clay took the idea for the Red-Headed League from the colour of his accomplice’s hair.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Peter Jones
snapshots.subtitle: Scotland Yard police agent
snapshots.body: Peter Jones, an official police agent from Scotland Yard whom Watson already knows. He is waiting with Holmes at Baker Street for the night’s expedition.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peter Jones
snapshots.subtitle: Scotland Yard police agent
snapshots.body: Peter Jones of Scotland Yard, self-important but, Holmes says, as brave as a bulldog and as tenacious as a lobster. In the bank cellar he handcuffs John Clay and takes him to the police station.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mr. Merryweather
snapshots.subtitle: Sad-faced, respectable gentleman on Holmes’s night expedition
snapshots.body: A long, thin, sad-faced man with a shiny hat and an oppressively respectable frock-coat, introduced by Holmes as a companion for the night’s adventure. He misses his Saturday-night game of cards.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Merryweather
snapshots.subtitle: Sad-faced, respectable gentleman on Holmes’s night expedition
snapshots.body: A long, thin, sad-faced man in an oppressively respectable frock-coat. Holmes explains that he is a bank director with a personal interest in the night’s business.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mr. Merryweather
snapshots.subtitle: Sad-faced, respectable gentleman on Holmes’s night expedition
snapshots.body: Chairman of directors of the City branch of a leading London bank. He leads the party into its cellar, where the bank keeps 30,000 French napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and has had warnings of an attempt on them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Ezekiah Hopkins
snapshots.subtitle: Founder of the Red-Headed League, according to its advertisement
snapshots.body: The late benefactor of Lebanon, Pennsylvania, named in the Red-Headed League’s advertisement; the notice says his bequest funds a vacancy paying £4 a week for nominal work.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ezekiah Hopkins
snapshots.subtitle: Founder of the Red-Headed League, according to its advertisement
snapshots.body: The late benefactor named in the Red-Headed League’s advertisement. According to Vincent Spaulding, he was an eccentric American millionaire, red-headed himself, who left his fortune in trust to provide easy, well-paid posts for red-headed men.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Sarasate
snapshots.subtitle: Spanish violinist (1844–1908)
snapshots.body: Pablo de Sarasate, the celebrated Spanish violin virtuoso and composer. Holmes takes Watson to hear him play at St. James’s Hall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gustave Flaubert
snapshots.subtitle: French novelist (1821–1880)
snapshots.body: French novelist, author of Madame Bovary. Holmes quotes a line he attributes to Flaubert’s letters to George Sand: ‘The man is nothing; the work is everything.’
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: George Sand
snapshots.subtitle: French novelist (1804–1876)
snapshots.body: Pen name of the French novelist Aurore Dupin, a friend and long-time correspondent of Gustave Flaubert.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary Sutherland
snapshots.subtitle: Holmes’s client; a short-sighted typist from Camberwell
snapshots.body: A client of Holmes’s whose “very simple problem” he mentions in passing. Her own case is told in A Case of Identity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary Sutherland
snapshots.subtitle: Holmes’s client; a short-sighted typist from Camberwell
snapshots.body: A young typist who lives with her mother and stepfather and has a small private income of her own. She comes to Holmes in distress because her fiancé disappeared on the morning of their wedding.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Hosmer Angel
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s vanished fiancé
snapshots.body: A shy, softly spoken gentleman with tinted glasses whom Mary Sutherland met at a ball and became engaged to. He vanished from his cab on the way to their wedding, and she wants Holmes to find him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hosmer Angel (false identity)
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s vanished fiancé
snapshots.body: Not a real man. Holmes shows that ‘Hosmer Angel’ was Mary’s stepfather, James Windibank, in disguise, with tinted glasses, false whiskers and a whispering voice. He used it, with his wife’s help, to court Mary himself and so keep her and her income at home.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mr. Windibank
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather
snapshots.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather, only about five years older than she is. He married her widowed mother and works as a travelling salesman for a wine importer. He refused to go to the police or to Holmes about her missing fiancé.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: James Windibank
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather
snapshots.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather. Holmes shows that, with his wife’s help, he disguised himself as ‘Hosmer Angel’ and courted Mary so that she, and the hundred a year he had the use of, would stay at home. He then vanished at the church door to leave her bound to a missing fiancé.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: James Windibank
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather
snapshots.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather, who disguised himself as ‘Hosmer Angel’ to keep her and her income at home. Faced with the evidence, he claimed it began as a joke and insisted that nothing he did was legally actionable. He fled when Holmes reached for a hunting crop.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mary Sutherland’s mother
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s mother
snapshots.body: Mary’s mother, a plumber’s widow who has remarried. Her new husband, Mr. Windibank, is nearly fifteen years younger than she is. She lives with him and Mary in Camberwell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary Sutherland’s mother
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s mother
snapshots.body: Mary’s mother, who remarried the much younger James Windibank. Holmes concludes that she knew of and helped with her husband’s disguise as ‘Hosmer Angel’, which explains her enthusiasm for the suitor.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mary Sutherland’s late father
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s late father, a plumber
snapshots.body: Mary’s father, now dead. He ran a plumbing business in the Tottenham Court Road, which her mother carried on for a time before selling it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Hardy
snapshots.subtitle: Former foreman of the Sutherland family’s plumbing business
snapshots.body: The foreman of the plumbing business left by Mary’s late father. He escorted Mary and her mother to the gasfitters’ ball.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Uncle Ned
snapshots.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s uncle in Auckland
snapshots.body: Mary’s uncle in Auckland, New Zealand. He left her £2,500 in New Zealand stock, and she receives only the interest from it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mrs. Etherege
snapshots.subtitle: Former client who recommended Holmes to Mary Sutherland
snapshots.body: An acquaintance of Mary’s whose husband Holmes found after the police had given him up for dead. She told Mary about Holmes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Westhouse & Marbank
snapshots.subtitle: Claret importers of Fenchurch Street
snapshots.body: A large firm of claret importers in Fenchurch Street. Mr. Windibank travels for them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Westhouse & Marbank
snapshots.subtitle: Claret importers of Fenchurch Street
snapshots.body: The claret importers of Fenchurch Street who employ James Windibank as a traveller. When Holmes sent them the Hosmer Angel description with the disguise removed, they replied that it matched Windibank in every respect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Balzac
snapshots.subtitle: French novelist (1799–1850)
snapshots.body: Honoré de Balzac, the French novelist. Holmes notes that Hosmer Angel’s letters quote him once.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hafiz
snapshots.subtitle: Fourteenth-century Persian poet
snapshots.body: The Persian poet Hafiz. Holmes cites ‘the old Persian saying’ and puts his wisdom on a level with Horace’s.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Horace
snapshots.subtitle: Roman poet (65–8 BC)
snapshots.body: The Latin poet Horace, whom Holmes pairs with Hafiz as a source of worldly wisdom.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Turner
snapshots.subtitle: Boscombe Valley landowner
snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, who made his fortune in Australia and came home to England some years ago. A widower with one daughter, he knew Charles McCarthy in the colonies and lets him Hatherley Farm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Turner
snapshots.subtitle: Boscombe Valley landowner
snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, an old acquaintance of Charles McCarthy from the Australian colonies and his landlord. Gravely ill, he comes to Holmes at the hotel; when Holmes says he knows all about McCarthy, Turner breaks down and says he would have spoken out rather than let young McCarthy be condemned.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Turner
snapshots.subtitle: Boscombe Valley landowner
snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, dying of diabetes. In a signed confession he tells Holmes that he was once the goldfields bushranger Black Jack of Ballarat; that Charles McCarthy, the convoy driver whose life he spared, later found him in England and blackmailed him for twenty years; and that he struck McCarthy down at Boscombe Pool when McCarthy pressed for James to marry his daughter Alice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Turner
snapshots.subtitle: Boscombe Valley landowner
snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley. He confessed to Holmes that he, once the bushranger Black Jack of Ballarat, killed his blackmailer Charles McCarthy at Boscombe Pool. Holmes kept the confession unused, and Turner lived seven months more before he died; his daughter never learned the truth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Charles McCarthy
snapshots.subtitle: Tenant of Hatherley Farm
snapshots.body: A former Australian colonist who rents Hatherley Farm from his old acquaintance John Turner. A widower with one son, James, he is said to be cold and forbidding in manner.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles McCarthy
snapshots.subtitle: Tenant of Hatherley Farm
snapshots.body: A former Australian colonist who rented Hatherley Farm from his old acquaintance John Turner, a widower with one son, James. On Monday 3 June he walked to Boscombe Pool for an important three o’clock appointment and never came back alive.

snapshots.name: Helen Stoner
snapshots.subtitle: Holmes’s client; Julia Stoner’s twin sister

snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s twin sister
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. She died two years ago at Stoke Moran, aged thirty, within a fortnight of her planned wedding to a major of marines she had met at her aunt’s.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Julia Stoner
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s twin sister
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. Two years ago, shortly before her wedding, she had been hearing a low whistle at night; then one stormy night she ran screaming from her locked room, cried out ‘It was the band! The speckled band!’ and died. The coroner found no cause of death.

snapshots.name: Julia Stoner
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s twin sister
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. Holmes concludes she was killed by a swamp adder that her stepfather sent through the ventilator and down the false bell-rope onto her bed; ‘the band’ was her description of the snake glimpsed by matchlight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
snapshots.body: A doctor and the last of the ancient Roylott family of Stoke Moran in Surrey. He is the stepfather of Helen Stoner, who lives with him in the old family house.

snapshots.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, last of the ruined Roylotts. He practised medicine in Calcutta, served a long prison term after beating his native butler to death, and married Helen’s widowed mother in India. Back at Stoke Moran he is feared for his violent temper, befriends only the wandering gipsies, and keeps a cheetah and a baboon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, a violent man who burst into Baker Street to threaten Holmes. Holmes has read his late wife’s will and finds that the stepdaughters’ marriages would sharply cut his income, which Holmes regards as a strong motive to prevent them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather. Holmes and Watson find him dead in his room, killed within seconds by a swamp adder coiled round his head; Holmes calls him a schemer who has fallen into the pit he dug for another.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
snapshots.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather. Holmes concludes that he killed Julia, and meant to kill Helen, by sending a trained swamp adder through the ventilator and down a false bell-rope, recalling it with a whistle; Holmes’s blows drove the snake back, and it bit him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

When Hatherley saw through the fuller’s-earth story, Stark locked him inside the hydraulic press and set it going. He then pursued him with a cleaver and cut off his thumb at the window. snapshots.name: Colonel Lysander Stark
snapshots.subtitle: Hatherley’s secretive client
snapshots.body: The thin, German-accented man who hired Hatherley as Colonel Lysander Stark and tried to kill him in the hydraulic press. Holmes suspects he did the same to a missing engineer, Jeremiah Hayling, a year earlier. Holmes concludes that Stark’s group are large-scale coiners who use the press to make false silver; the police had already been hunting such a gang. The woman called him ‘Fritz’.

snapshots.body: A prominent London banker who accepted the Beryl Coronet as security for a £50,000 loan to an illustrious client and took it home to Streatham. After catching his son Arthur with the damaged coronet at night, he handed him to the police and has come to Holmes for help.

snapshots.body: A prominent London banker who accepted the Beryl Coronet as security for a loan to an illustrious client. Holmes recovered the three missing stones for him, showed that Arthur had been wrongly accused, and told him that his niece Mary had fled with Sir George Burnwell.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, whom his father admits to having spoiled. Charming but wild, he has run up gambling debts through an aristocratic club and the influence of his friend Sir George Burnwell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, with gambling debts and a worldly friend in Sir George Burnwell. His father found him at night holding the damaged Beryl Coronet with three beryls missing; Arthur refused to explain and was taken into police custody.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, arrested after his father found him with the damaged Beryl Coronet. Holmes has told Holder that Arthur did not take the stones and that he is owed a humble apology.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, wrongly arrested over the damaged Beryl Coronet. He had seen his cousin Mary hand the coronet out of a window, chased Sir George Burnwell down the lane and wrestled it back, minus one fragment. He stayed silent to protect Mary’s secret.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mary Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece, whom he adopted when her father died five years ago and treats as a daughter. She runs his household and has twice refused Arthur’s proposals of marriage.

snapshots.name: Mary Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter, who ran his household. She has left Fairbank overnight, leaving a note saying she brought trouble on her uncle and begging him not to search for her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mary Holder

snapshots.name: Mary Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter. Persuaded by her secret lover Sir George Burnwell, she took the Beryl Coronet from her uncle’s bureau at night and handed it out of the hall window to him. She has since fled with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Sir George Burnwell
snapshots.subtitle: Arthur Holder’s worldly older friend
snapshots.body: Arthur’s older friend, a handsome, much-travelled man of the world and a brilliant talker, whose influence keeps drawing Arthur back to gambling. Holder finds him fascinating in person but says his cynicism makes him distrust him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sir George Burnwell
snapshots.subtitle: Arthur Holder’s worldly older friend
snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend and a frequent visitor at Holder’s house. Holmes reveals that he had a secret understanding with Holder’s niece Mary and that the two have fled together.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Sir George Burnwell
snapshots.subtitle: Arthur Holder’s worldly older friend
snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend, whom Holmes calls a ruined gambler and one of the most dangerous men in England. He received the Beryl Coronet from Mary at the hall window; Arthur chased him down the lane, cut him over the eye and wrested the coronet back, leaving a fragment in his hands.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Sir George Burnwell
snapshots.subtitle: Arthur Holder’s worldly older friend
snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend, who took the Beryl Coronet with Mary’s help and fled with her. Holmes traced him by his boots, confronted him at pistol-point and learned he had sold the three stones for £600; Holmes bought them back and promised no prosecution to avoid scandal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.subtitle: Second waiting-maid in the Holder household
snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid, in service only a few months but with excellent references. She is very pretty and has admirers who sometimes hang about the house.

snapshots.name: Lucy Parr
snapshots.subtitle: Second waiting-maid in the Holder household
snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid, in service only a few months. She served the coffee while Holder spoke of the coronet, and Mary saw her slip out to meet her sweetheart, the greengrocer Francis Prosper; Mary suggests she may have passed on what she overheard.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Lucy Parr
snapshots.subtitle: Second waiting-maid in the Holder household
snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid. Holmes confirmed from the snow and from inquiry that her night outing was simply a meeting with her sweetheart at the kitchen door, and ruled out the maids as the coronet’s takers.

snapshots.subtitle: Greengrocer who delivers to the Holder house
snapshots.body: The greengrocer who brings the Holders their vegetables. Mary saw him in the dark at the kitchen door with the maid Lucy Parr on the night of the theft.

snapshots.subtitle: Greengrocer who delivers to the Holder house
snapshots.body: The greengrocer who delivers to the Holders and Lucy Parr’s sweetheart. Holmes guessed his wooden leg from the tracks at the kitchen door, and confirmed that he and Lucy had only met there to talk.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.body: A visitor bearing ‘one of the highest, noblest, most exalted names in England’, whom Holder declines to name even to Holmes. He borrows £50,000 from Holder’s bank and leaves the Beryl Coronet as security, promising to reclaim it on Monday.

snapshots.name: Violet Hunter
snapshots.subtitle: A London governess; Holmes’s client in this story
snapshots.body: She took the post at the Copper Beeches, where the Rucastles had her wear an electric-blue dress and sit with her back to the window, and she found a locked, barricaded wing. Frightened by Rucastle’s threats, she has summoned Holmes to Winchester.

snapshots.name: Violet Hunter
snapshots.subtitle: A London governess; Holmes’s client in this story
snapshots.body: She helped Holmes and Watson search the locked wing at the Copper Beeches. Watson later reports that she became head of a private school at Walsall, with considerable success.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: A very stout, smiling Hampshire gentleman who offers Violet Hunter an unusually high salary to be governess to his young son, on condition that she cut her hair short and humour his wife’s little whims.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: Holmes now believes Rucastle hired Violet Hunter to impersonate his daughter, Alice, whom he suspects is locked in the barricaded room rather than in America, and that the window performances were meant to deceive the man watching from the road.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: Caught by Holmes in the empty locked room, Rucastle ran for his mastiff, but the starving dog attacked him instead. Watson shot it, and Rucastle was carried inside alive but badly mauled.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that he kept his daughter Alice prisoner to stop her marrying and taking control of money left to her by will, and hired Violet Hunter to drive away her suitor, Mr. Fowler. His mastiff mauled him when he set it loose.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: He kept his daughter Alice prisoner for her money and was mauled by his own mastiff. He survived as a broken man, cared for by his devoted wife, and still lives with his old servants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Mrs. Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s second wife
snapshots.body: Rucastle’s pale, silent wife, much younger than he is, devoted to her husband and little son. Violet Hunter is told the job’s odd requests are her wishes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mrs. Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s second wife
snapshots.body: After her husband was mauled by the mastiff, she nursed him; Watson reports that he survived as a broken man, kept alive only by her care.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Alice Rucastle

snapshots.body: Rucastle’s grown daughter. In his letter he says she is now in Philadelphia, and Violet Hunter is to wear a dress that belonged to her.

snapshots.name: Alice Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s daughter by his first marriage
snapshots.body: Rucastle says she went to Philadelphia because she disliked her stepmother. Holmes now believes she never left: he thinks she is the prisoner in the barricaded room, and that Violet was hired to impersonate her.

snapshots.name: Alice Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s daughter by his first marriage
snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that Alice’s father imprisoned her. A will gave her money, and he wanted it kept from her suitor, Mr. Fowler. When she refused to sign it over, his pressure brought on brain-fever, and her hair was cut off during the illness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Alice Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s daughter by his first marriage
snapshots.body: She escaped through the skylight with Mr. Fowler’s help. They married by special licence in Southampton the next day, and he now holds a government post in Mauritius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.subtitle: The family at the Copper Beeches

snapshots.body: The Rucastles’ rough, grizzled manservant and groom, often drunk, and the only one who can manage the mastiff, Carlo, which he lets loose at night.

snapshots.subtitle: Groom and manservant at the Copper Beeches

snapshots.subtitle: Alice Rucastle’s suitor, a seaman
snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms Holmes’s account. Fowler, a persistent seaman, kept watch on the house, won her over with gifts, kept her husband supplied with drink, and had a ladder ready to rescue Alice once Rucastle went out.

snapshots.name: Mr. Fowler
snapshots.subtitle: Alice Rucastle’s suitor, a seaman

snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, born in New Jersey in 1858, once prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw and now retired and living in London. snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, formerly prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw, now living at Briony Lodge, St. John’s Wood. She holds a compromising photograph of herself with the King of Bohemia. She has just married the lawyer Godfrey Norton in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica, with Holmes, in his groom’s disguise, pulled in as witness.

snapshots.name: Irene Adler
snapshots.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
snapshots.body: An American-born opera singer who outwits Holmes. She saw through his clergyman act after the fire alarm, followed him home in men’s clothes to wish him good night, and left England with her new husband, Godfrey Norton. In her letter, signed ‘Irene Norton, née Adler’, she promises not to trouble the King, keeping the photograph only for her own protection.

He is about to announce his betrothal to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen and wants Holmes to recover a compromising photograph of himself with Irene Adler, which she has threatened to send to his bride’s family.

snapshots.body: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, hereditary King of Bohemia. Irene Adler’s letter convinces him she will never use the photograph, and he declares himself satisfied. He gives Holmes her portrait as a reward; Holmes takes it but coldly ignores the King’s outstretched hand.

snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant, who works for half wages to learn the business. He showed Wilson the Red-Headed League’s advertisement, urged him to apply, and pushed him through the crowd of applicants. snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding
snapshots.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant: a small, quick, beardless man of about thirty with an acid stain on his forehead and pierced ears. snapshots.body: The name John Clay used while working as Jabez Wilson’s assistant. Holmes explains that he took the job at half wages, urged Wilson to apply to the sham League, and used the hours Wilson was away to dig a tunnel from the cellar to the bank behind the shop.

snapshots.body: A young master criminal—murderer, thief, coiner and forger—whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard names as the man he most wants to arrest. Jones says Clay has royal ancestry, went to Eton and Oxford, and has never been seen by him despite years of pursuit.

snapshots.name: John Clay

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard has hunted for years. Caught climbing up through the floor of the bank cellar, he is handcuffed by Jones, insists on his royal blood, and is led off coolly to the police station.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: John Clay
snapshots.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal caught tunnelling into the bank cellar and arrested by Peter Jones. Holmes explains that Clay, under the name Vincent Spaulding, had worked as Jabez Wilson’s assistant and devised the Red-Headed League with a red-haired accomplice to get Wilson out of the shop each day.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ross

snapshots.body: The man who ran the Red-Headed League’s office and hired Jabez Wilson. Holmes explains that the League was a scheme by John Clay and his red-haired accomplice to keep Wilson away from his shop: one rogue kept the temporary office while the other urged Wilson to apply.

In a signed confession he tells Holmes that he was once the goldfields bushranger Black Jack of Ballarat; that Charles McCarthy, the convoy driver whose life he spared, later found him in England and blackmailed him for twenty years; and that he struck McCarthy down at Boscombe Pool when McCarthy pressed for James to marry his daughter Alice.

snapshots.name: John Turner

snapshots.body: A prominent London banker who accepted the Beryl Coronet as security for a £50,000 loan to an illustrious client and took it home to Streatham. After catching his son Arthur with the damaged coronet at night, he handed him to the police and has come to Holmes for help.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, with gambling debts and a worldly friend in Sir George Burnwell. His father found him at night holding the damaged Beryl Coronet with three beryls missing; Arthur refused to explain and was taken into police custody.

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder

snapshots.name: Arthur Holder
snapshots.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, wrongly arrested over the damaged Beryl Coronet. He had seen his cousin Mary hand the coronet out of a window, chased Sir George Burnwell down the lane and wrestled it back, minus one fragment. He stayed silent to protect Mary’s secret.

He received the Beryl Coronet from Mary at the hall window; Arthur chased him down the lane, cut him over the eye and wrested the coronet back, leaving a fragment in his hands.

snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend, who took the Beryl Coronet with Mary’s help and fled with her. Holmes traced him by his boots, confronted him at pistol-point and learned he had sold the three stones for £600; Holmes bought them back and promised no prosecution to avoid scandal.

snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid, in service only a few months. She served the coffee while Holder spoke of the coronet, and Mary saw her slip out to meet her sweetheart, the greengrocer Francis Prosper; Mary suggests she may have passed on what she overheard.

snapshots.body: She took the post at the Copper Beeches, where the Rucastles had her wear an electric-blue dress and sit with her back to the window, and she found a locked, barricaded wing. Frightened by Rucastle’s threats, she has summoned Holmes to Winchester.

snapshots.body: A very stout, smiling Hampshire gentleman who offers Violet Hunter an unusually high salary to be governess to his young son, on condition that she cut her hair short and humour his wife’s little whims.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: Caught by Holmes in the empty locked room, Rucastle ran for his mastiff, but the starving dog attacked him instead. Watson shot it, and Rucastle was carried inside alive but badly mauled.

snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that he kept his daughter Alice prisoner to stop her marrying and taking control of money left to her by will, and hired Violet Hunter to drive away her suitor, Mr. Fowler. His mastiff mauled him when he set it loose.

snapshots.name: Jephro Rucastle
snapshots.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
snapshots.body: He kept his daughter Alice prisoner for her money and was mauled by his own mastiff. He survived as a broken man, cared for by his devoted wife, and still lives with his old servants.

snapshots.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s second wife

snapshots.name: Alice Rucastle

snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that Alice’s father imprisoned her. A will gave her money, and he wanted it kept from her suitor, Mr. Fowler. When she refused to sign it over, his pressure brought on brain-fever, and her hair was cut off during the illness.

snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms Holmes’s account. Fowler, a persistent seaman, kept watch on the house, won her over with gifts, kept her husband supplied with drink, and had a ladder ready to rescue Alice once Rucastle went out.
